Respiratory Illness Outbreak Disrupts Steel Production in Hebei, Operations Resume After Quarantine Lifted

SHIJIAZHUANG, China, June 12 — Steel production in China’s Hebei province has resumed after a respiratory illness outbreak among workers prompted partial site closures and quarantines at several major mills, local authorities and industry sources said Wednesday.

The outbreak, which began in late May at the Baolin Steelworks complex in Tangshan, affected more than 400 workers across five facilities, according to the Hebei Provincial Health Commission. The illness, identified as a severe strain of adenovirus, led to high fever, cough, and in some cases pneumonia, causing concern among local officials and steel industry unions.

Production at the affected sites was reduced for over a week as infected workers were isolated and close contacts quarantined, prompting delays in shipment and order fulfillment. "At the height of the outbreak, we had to suspend operations on two blast furnaces for disinfection and to prevent further spread," said Wang Xin, spokesperson for Baolin Steelworks. "This was necessary to protect our workforce and the wider community."

The Hebei Steel Industry Association estimated that regional crude steel output fell by nearly 12% in the first week of June compared to the monthly average, with daily production dropping by roughly 30,000 metric tons. "Supply chain disruptions were limited but noticeable, especially for downstream customers relying on just-in-time deliveries," said analyst Zhao Yifan at GreenCrest Metals Research.

Authorities declared the outbreak contained on June 10, following a mass testing campaign and a week-long closure of the most affected mill sections. "All workers have now tested negative, and production has gradually resumed under enhanced hygiene protocols," said Li Jia, deputy director of the provincial health commission.

No fatalities were reported, though 14 workers required hospital treatment. Local trade unions praised the rapid response but called for stronger health protections. "We appreciate the swift action by employers and health officials, but more investment in worker safety is critical," said Liu Meng, union representative at Tangshan Steel Federation.

With operations back to normal, analysts expect Hebei’s steel output to stabilize by month’s end. “The disruption was significant but short-lived,” said Zhao. “We do not foresee long-term impacts on annual production targets at this time.”
